summary: Specifies a sockets API for advanced IPv6 applications, as a supplement to the basic API in RFC 3493. It targets programs such as ping, traceroute, and routing daemons that need raw sockets and access to IPv6 and ICMPv6 header fields. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives IPv6 programmers a portable way to access packet details needed by tools and network software. It covers raw sockets, extension headers, interface information, and path MTU controls.

subtitle: Socket interfaces for IPv6 programs that need raw packets, extension headers, or path MTU details.

tldr.problem: IPv6 applications such as ping, traceroute, and routing daemons need consistent access to packet details that the basic sockets API does not provide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines common header structures, raw-socket behavior, ancillary data and socket options for packet information and extension headers, plus path MTU controls.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3542 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2292. It does not define access to the IP authentication or encapsulating security payload headers.

sections.title: Why an Advanced IPv6 Sockets API
sections.content:
The basic IPv6 sockets API covers TCP and UDP applications. This document defines additional interfaces for applications such as ping, traceroute, and routing daemons that need access to IPv6 or ICMPv6 header information.

IPv4 raw-socket programs were often portable because implementations shared Berkeley code or header files. IPv6 had no common implementation base, so the RFC defines common structures and behavior. It updates and replaces RFC 2292 and does not cover application access to the authentication or encapsulating security payload headers.
sections.plainLanguage: This API standardizes how specialized programs access IPv6 packet details. It supplements the basic socket interfaces for TCP and UDP applications.

sections.title: Shared IPv6 and ICMPv6 Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC defines common C structures and constants in <netinet/ip6.h> and <netinet/icmp6.h>. These describe IPv6 and ICMPv6 headers, extension headers, protocol values, and message types. Header fields remain in network byte order.

These shared definitions let applications refer to packet fields and message types consistently across implementations. The document also defines address comparison and protocol-name support for applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs need agreed names and structures to read packet fields. These headers provide common definitions for IPv6 and ICMPv6.

sections.title: Raw Sockets and Checksum Handling
sections.content:
IPv6 raw sockets bypass TCP or UDP and let an application send or receive data for protocols handled directly by the application. Their data is in network byte order. Unlike the IPv4 interface described in the RFC, an IPv6 raw socket does not send or receive a complete packet with all extension headers; ancillary data carries those headers and other selected fields.

The kernel calculates the mandatory ICMPv6 checksum for ICMPv6 raw sockets. For other raw IPv6 sockets, an application can set IPV6_CHECKSUM so the kernel calculates and verifies a checksum at a specified offset. An ICMPv6 type filter lets an application select which message types it receives; all types pass by default.
sections.plainLanguage: A raw socket gives an application direct access to a network protocol's data. The kernel handles ICMPv6 checksums, and an application can filter which ICMPv6 types it receives.

sections.title: Packet Information and Extension Headers
sections.content:
An application can send or receive packet details such as the source or destination address, interface, hop limit, next hop, traffic class, and selected IPv6 extension headers. It can pass information for one datagram as ancillary data with sendmsg() or recvmsg(), or set sticky socket options that apply to packets until changed.

When the application enables a receive option, the kernel returns the requested information as ancillary data. A per-message ancillary item overrides a sticky option of the same type for that datagram. Helper functions build and inspect Routing headers and Hop-by-Hop or Destination options.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can attach packet settings to one datagram or set defaults for a socket. It can also request packet details and use helper functions for extension headers.

sections.title: Path MTU Controls and Security
sections.content:
Applications can control whether packets use path MTU discovery or the minimum IPv6 MTU with IPV6_USE_MIN_MTU. UDP and raw sockets can disable automatic fragmentation with IPV6_DONTFRAG, receive path MTU information, and query the current path MTU on a connected socket.

The security section says some Hop-by-Hop and Destination options may be restricted to privileged processes. Systems must also prevent non-privileged processes from using IPV6_PKTINFO to specify an arbitrary source address.
sections.plainLanguage: These options let a program learn or control the packet size used on a path. Systems should restrict options that could let an unprivileged program use a false source address.
